task.title: Relics: create and edit relics on one machine
task.description:
A relic is a new kind of record in Workbook, separate from tasks. It holds specs, plans, decisions, transcripts and similar material, with the same history and sharing that tasks have. A relic has a title, a type, an author, links, and content made of named parts.

This is the first relic story. It defines the record and its storage, and makes relics usable on one machine from the command line. Nothing is shared yet. The format decided here is permanent, so it is the story to get right.

## The record

```json
{
  "id": "WB-R-01M9…",
  "title": "Task archive compaction",
  "type": "spec",
  "schema": null,
  "author": "dylan@example.com",
  "retired": false,
  "deleted": false,
  "properties": { "status": "approved" },
  "parts": [
    { "id": "01M9…A", "type": "section",
      "fields": { "heading": "Goals" },
      "body": { "format": "md", "version": "<change id>", "bytes": 1840 } },
    { "id": "01M9…B", "type": "decision",
      "fields": { "question": "By hand or on a timer?", "chosen": "by hand" } }
  ],
  "links": []
}
```

- **Enforced by Workbook:** title, type, author, history, the retired and deleted marks, and (from the schema story on) the schema version the relic names. Author is recorded from whoever creates the relic and is not editable. Every later edit carries its own author.
- **Defined by the project:** properties (named values on the whole relic) and parts.
- **Parts** are an ordered, flat list. Each part has a permanent ID, a part type, small structured `fields`, and an optional text `body` stored exactly as written. Parts are never nested.
- **Body format** is a short label saved with the body, written like a file ending (`md`, `html`, `txt`, `json`, `ts`). It tells a viewer how to draw the body. Workbook never checks the text against it. `--body-file notes.md` takes the label from the file ending unless `--body-format` says otherwise. A body with no label is plain text.
- **Relic ID:** the project key, `-R-`, and a unique ID, for example `WB-R-01M9…`. A project key cannot contain a hyphen and a task's unique part always starts with a digit, so `WB-R-` is never the start of a task ID. Tests prove a task ID is never parsed as a relic ID or the reverse.
- **Part address:** `<relic-id>#<part-id>`. Any unambiguous prefix works on the command line, as for tasks.
- **Removing a part hides it.** It is not destroyed, and it can be restored.
- No schema exists yet, so any type name, property, part type and field is accepted within the size limits. The record leaves room to name a schema version later.

## Storage in Git

Relics follow the task model: one private ref per relic, a chain of unchangeable commits, each holding the change that was made and the resulting state.

```
refs/workbook/relics/WB-R-01M9…
 └── commit                      (parent: the previous change)
      └── tree
           ├── operation.json    the change that was made
           ├── state.json        enforced fields, properties, and the part list
           │                     (ID, type, position, body format, current version)
           ├── links.json        the relic's links (empty in this story)
           └── parts/
                ├── 01M9…A/
                │    ├── fields.json
                │    └── body
                └── 01M9…B/
                     └── fields.json
```

- Each part's fields and body are their own Git objects, so editing one part of a 500-part relic writes only that part's objects.
- Every commit lists all current parts, so a relic at any point in its history is complete on its own.
- No single stored object grows with the relic's whole content. Workbook refuses to read any object over 4 MiB, so the part list and links stay small and the content sits beside them.
- Deleting a relic records a delete marker. The ref is never removed, and `restore` brings the relic back.
- Every stored format carries a version from this first release.

## Changes a relic can record

| Area | Changes |
| --- | --- |
| Relic | create, set title, delete, restore |
| Properties | set one, clear one |
| Parts | add, set one field, clear one field, set body (with its format and the version it started from), move, remove, restore |

One command may record several of these together. They are stored as one commit and applied together or not at all. Retire, schema moves, links, merged bodies and checkpoints are added by later stories. Reserve their place in the format so adding them needs no rewrite.

## Body versions

- Each saved text of a body has a version name: the ID of the change that saved it. It does not depend on Git commit IDs, which change when history is replayed.
- Every body edit records the version it started from (`--base <version>`). This is in the format from the first release, because it cannot be added to old edits later.
- An edit whose starting version is not the current one is refused by the command. There is no overwrite option. To replace a body on purpose, read the current version and save over it.
- The same check is made again whenever a relic's current text is worked out from its history: a body edit counts only if the version it names was the current one at that point. An edit that fails stays in history under its author and does not change the text. This protects against a bug, another tool, or a direct write to Git, and makes every clone arrive at the same text.

## Part order

- A part's position is an exact fraction, as task ranks are, so a part can always be placed between two others.
- Unlike tasks, a new position is the shortest fraction that fits in the gap, not the midpoint. Repeated inserts at one spot then grow slowly.
- A position is limited to 256 bytes. A placement that would pass the limit is refused with a clear message.
- A part is placed with `--before <part>` or `--after <part>`. With neither, a new part goes at the end.

## Starting size limits

Limits are part of the storage format. They can be raised later and never lowered.

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Title | 500 bytes |
| Type name, part type name | 100 bytes each |
| Body format label | 16 bytes |
| One part's position | 256 bytes |
| All properties of one relic | 64 KiB |
| One part's fields | 16 KiB |
| One part's body | 1 MiB |
| Live parts per relic | 2,000 |
| All current bodies of one relic together | 16 MiB |

The size of one item is checked when it is saved and again when it is read. Counts and totals are checked only when something is being added, never when a relic is read, so a relic can never become unreadable.

## Commands

```
workbook relic create "Title" --type spec [--from-file relic.json]
workbook relic list   [--type T]
workbook relic show   <relic>[#part] [--body]
workbook relic update <relic> [--title …] [--set name=value] [--clear name]
                      [--add-part --part-type T --field k=v --body-file f --body-format F
                                  (--before <part> | --after <part>)]
                      [--part <part> --field k=v --body-file f --body-format F --base <version>]
                      [--move-part <part> (--before <part> | --after <part>)]
                      [--remove-part <part>]
workbook relic delete | restore <relic>
workbook relic export <relic>
```

- Every command takes `--json`.
- `create --from-file` takes a whole relic as one JSON document. `export` writes one. A relic exported and created again from that file has the same content.
- `workbook validate` checks relic history as it checks task history.
- `workbook next`, `list` and `board` never return relics.

## Done when

- A relic with many parts can be created, read, edited part by part, reordered, deleted and restored on one machine, with JSON output throughout.
- A body edit from an out-of-date version is refused, and a stale edit written straight into history changes nothing when the relic is read.
- Tests cover root and linear relic histories, replay giving the same state in any order, duplicate delivery, every limit, both Git hash formats where the machine supports them, and an interrupted write.
- No task command changes behavior, and an agent asking for its next task is never handed a relic.

## Not in this story

Sharing with `origin`, the SQLite index, links, schemas, history and diff commands, retiring, compaction and the web page. Each has its own story. Reads in this story may come straight from Git.

## Where the design is

The approved design is "Workbook Relics Design" (2026-11-21). It is kept out of the repository. Until "Relics: teach agents to use relics and store the design as the first relic" is done, an untracked copy sits at `specs/2026-11-21-relics-design.html` in Dylan's checkout. After that, read the relic. This description carries what the story needs, and the design wins where the two disagree.
